subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
skillName: Gather relevant information from multiple sources
intro: Good research means gathering the right information from sources you can trust. To do that well you have to do four things. First, decide whether a source is relevant, meaning it actually answers your research question instead of just mentioning the topic. Second, judge whether a source is credible by asking who wrote it, when, why, and what evidence it offers. A recent report from a government or university expert is usually stronger than an ad or a stranger's opinion. Third, decide when to quote a source word for word with quotation marks and when to paraphrase by restating the idea in your own words. Fourth, avoid plagiarism. Swapping a few words while keeping the original sentence is still plagiarism, and so is copying without quotation marks or credit. Finally, give a basic citation so a reader can find your source: author, title, source or website name, and date. This lesson walks through each of these skills.

items.prompt:
Research question: How do honeybees help farmers grow crops? You find four sources. Which one is most relevant to the question?
A) "Honeybee Pollination and Crop Yields," a guide from a university farming program
B) "Top Ten Honey Dessert Recipes," a food blog
C) "The History of Beekeeping Hats," a hobby website
D) "How to Remove a Wasp Nest," a pest control company ad

steps: Look back at the exact question: it asks how honeybees help farmers grow crops. The key idea is bees and crops, not bees in general.
Source A is about pollination and crop yields, which is exactly how bees help crops grow. It directly answers the question.
Source B mentions honey but is about dessert recipes, which has nothing to do with growing crops. It is off topic.
Source C is about beekeeping hats, a hobby detail that does not explain how bees help crops. Off topic.
Source D is about wasps, not honeybees, and is about removing nests, not helping crops. Off topic.
A source is relevant only if it answers the research question, not just because it mentions the topic. Only A does that.
solution.answer: A) "Honeybee Pollination and Crop Yields," a guide from a university farming program

items.prompt:
Research question: Is the local river safe to swim in? You have two sources.
Source 1: A report on the state environmental agency website (a .gov site), updated this year, that lists recent water test results.
Source 2: A comment on a social media post from a user who writes, "I think it is fine, I swam once and felt okay."
Which source is more credible, and why?

steps: To judge credibility, ask who wrote it, when, why, and what evidence it offers.
Source 1 comes from a state environmental agency, which has expert authority on water safety. The .gov site signals an official agency.
Source 1 is also recent (updated this year) and offers tested evidence, the actual water test results.
Source 2 is one person's opinion based on swimming a single time. There is no expertise, no testing, and no evidence beyond a personal feeling.
Sounding confident does not make a source credible. Expertise, recent date, and real evidence do.
Source 1 is more credible because it is written by experts, is current, and is backed by tested evidence rather than a single opinion.
solution.answer: Source 1, the state environmental agency report, because it comes from experts, is recent, and is backed by water test results rather than one person's opinion.

items.prompt:
You are writing a report and found this source sentence: "Most of the oxygen we breathe is produced by ocean plants, not trees." Which choice is an accurate paraphrase in your own words?
A) Ocean plants, rather than trees, make most of the oxygen people breathe.
B) Most of the oxygen we breathe is produced by ocean plants, not trees.
C) Trees make most of the oxygen that people breathe.
D) The ocean is very large and full of many kinds of plants.

steps: A paraphrase restates the source's idea in new words while keeping the same meaning.
Choice A says ocean plants, not trees, make most of the oxygen. That keeps the meaning but uses different words. It is a correct paraphrase.
Choice B is copied word for word from the source, so it is not a paraphrase at all.
Choice C changes the meaning by claiming trees make the most oxygen, which is the opposite of the source. A paraphrase must not change the meaning.
Choice D talks about the ocean's size and does not state the source's main idea, so it is off topic.
Only A restates the idea accurately in the student's own words.
solution.answer: A) Ocean plants, rather than trees, make most of the oxygen people breathe.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: "Volcanic ash can travel thousands of miles and disrupt air travel." A student wrote this in a report with no quotation marks and no credit: "Volcanic ash can move thousands of miles and disrupt air travel." Is this plagiarism, and why?

steps: Compare the student's sentence to the original word by word.
The student kept the same sentence structure and almost all of the same words, changing only "travel" to "move."
Swapping one or two words while keeping the original structure is still plagiarism, not a real paraphrase.
There are also no quotation marks and no credit to the source, so even an exact copy would be plagiarism.
A real fix would either quote it exactly with quotation marks and credit, or fully restate the idea, for example: "Ash from a volcano can spread across long distances and interfere with flights."
So yes, the student's version is plagiarism because it only swaps a word, keeps the original sentence, and gives no credit.
solution.answer: Yes, it is plagiarism. Changing only "travel" to "move" while keeping the same sentence, with no quotation marks and no credit, is still copying.

items.prompt: A complete citation should include the author, the title, the source or website name, and the date. Look at this citation a student wrote: "\"Saving the Coral Reefs.\" 2022." Which bibliographic elements are missing?

steps: List the four parts a basic citation needs: author, title, source or website name, and date.
Check what the student's citation includes: it has the title, "Saving the Coral Reefs," and the date, 2022.
It does not name the author, so the reader cannot tell who wrote it.
It also does not name the source or website where it was published, so the reader cannot find where it appeared.
A citation that lists only a title and date is not complete, even though those parts are correct.
A complete version would read: Maria Lopez. "Saving the Coral Reefs." Ocean Today. 2022.
solution.answer: The author and the source or website name are missing. The citation has only the title and the date.

items.prompt:
Research question: What did ancient Egyptians eat? Which source is most relevant to the question?
A) "Daily Meals in Ancient Egypt," an article from a museum's history department
B) "Plan Your Trip to Egypt Today," a travel agency ad
C) "Modern Egyptian Pop Music," a music magazine
D) "How Pyramids Were Built," a documentary website
items.hint: Reread the exact question. It asks about food in ancient Egypt, not travel, music, or pyramids. Pick the source that answers that.

steps: The question asks what ancient Egyptians ate, so the key idea is food in ancient Egypt.
Source A is about daily meals in ancient Egypt, which directly answers the question.
Source B is a travel ad, C is about modern music, and D is about building pyramids. None of these explain what people ate.
Only A answers the research question, so it is the most relevant.
solution.answer: A) "Daily Meals in Ancient Egypt," an article from a museum's history department

items.prompt:
Research question: Do school start times affect how well students learn? You have two sources.
Source 1: A study published this year by a university sleep research center, based on data from 5,000 students.
Source 2: A blog post from last week titled "Why I Hate Mornings," where the writer shares personal feelings about waking up early.
Which source is more credible, and why?
items.hint: Ask who wrote each source, why they wrote it, and what evidence they give. Expertise and real data beat personal feelings.

steps: Both sources are recent, so date does not decide it here. Look at author, purpose, and evidence.
Source 1 is from a university sleep research center, which is an expert source, and it is based on data from 5,000 students.
Source 2 is a personal blog about the writer's feelings, with no expertise and no evidence beyond opinion.
Although both are recent, Source 1 has expert authors and real data, so it is more credible.
solution.answer: Source 1, the university study, because it is written by experts and is backed by data from 5,000 students rather than personal feelings.

items.prompt:
Source sentence: "A tornado's wind speed can reach 300 miles per hour." Which choice is an accurate paraphrase in your own words?
A) Tornado winds can blow as fast as 300 miles per hour.
B) A tornado's wind speed can reach 300 miles per hour.
C) Tornadoes are dangerous storms that scare many people.
D) A tornado's wind speed can reach 30 miles per hour.
items.hint: A paraphrase keeps the same meaning, including the exact number, but uses different words. Watch for choices that copy or change the facts.

steps: A paraphrase restates the idea in new words while keeping the meaning and the facts the same.
Choice A says tornado winds can blow as fast as 300 miles per hour, which keeps the meaning and the number but uses different words. It is a correct paraphrase.
Choice B copies the source word for word, so it is not a paraphrase.
Choice C does not state the wind speed at all, so it leaves out the main idea.
Choice D changes 300 to 30, which changes the fact, so it is wrong.
Only A is an accurate paraphrase.
solution.answer: A) Tornado winds can blow as fast as 300 miles per hour.

items.prompt: Original source sentence: "Sea turtles can live for more than 100 years in the wild." A student wrote this in a report with no quotation marks and no credit: "Sea turtles can survive for more than 100 years in the wild." Is this plagiarism, and why?
items.hint: Compare the two sentences. Did the student really restate the idea, or just swap a word while keeping the original sentence?

steps: Compare the student's sentence to the original.
The student kept the same structure and nearly all the same words, changing only "live" to "survive."
Swapping one word while keeping the original sentence is still plagiarism, not a real paraphrase.
There are also no quotation marks and no credit, so it would be plagiarism even as an exact copy.
A real fix would restate the idea fully, such as: "In the wild, some sea turtles reach an age of over a century," or quote it exactly with quotation marks and credit.
solution.answer: Yes, it is plagiarism. Changing only "live" to "survive" while keeping the same sentence, with no quotation marks and no credit, is still copying.

items.prompt: A complete citation should include the author, the title, the source or website name, and the date. Look at this citation a student wrote: "Carlos Reyes. \"The Science of Volcanoes.\" Earth Now." Which bibliographic element is missing?
items.hint: Check the citation against the four parts: author, title, source or website name, and date. Which part is not there?

steps: List the four parts a citation needs: author, title, source or website name, and date.
The student's citation has the author (Carlos Reyes), the title ("The Science of Volcanoes"), and the source name (Earth Now).
It does not include the date, so a reader cannot tell when it was published or how current it is.
A complete version would add the year, for example: Carlos Reyes. "The Science of Volcanoes." Earth Now. 2023.
solution.answer: The date is missing. The citation has the author, title, and source name but no date.
